q: This painting's composition includes a mirror on the back wall reflecting the faces of the king and queen, Philip IV and Mariana. Its artist portrays himself at an easel holding a brush, beside a five-year-old Infanta Margarita Teresa and her attendants. A dog sleeps in the foreground near a dwarf. For 10 points, name this Diego Velazquez painting whose title refers to ladies-in-waiting.

This artist worked with his brother Hubert on the Ghent Altarpiece, a polyptych in Saint Bavo Cathedral. His Arnolfini Portrait includes a convex mirror and the inscription "was here." He perfected oil glazes for jewel-like color. For 10 points, name this early Netherlandish painter.

This painter's Calling of Saint Matthew in the Contarelli Chapel uses a beam of light from a high window. He used dramatic chiaroscuro, painted Judith Beheading Holofernes, and fled Rome after killing a man in 1606. He died on the way back from exile in Malta and Naples. For 10 points, name this Italian Baroque painter, known by his hometown's name.

This artist's triptych in the Prado shows Eden on the left panel, a pleasure-filled landscape in the center, and a hellish landscape on the right. His other works include The Haywain and The Temptation of Saint Anthony. His fantastic imagery of hybrid monsters later influenced Surrealists. For 10 points, name this Dutch painter of The Garden of Earthly Delights.

This painting, now in Madrid's Reina Sofia museum, was shown at the 1937 Paris World's Fair. A bull, a screaming horse, a dead soldier holding a broken sword, and a woman carrying a lamp are depicted in gray, black, and white. It responds to the bombing of a Basque town. For 10 points, name this mural-sized Pablo Picasso work.

This painter was a founder of the Vienna Secession. He covered portraits like Adele Bloch-Bauer I in gold leaf, and he painted The Kiss during his "golden phase." His Beethoven Frieze was made for a Secession exhibition. For 10 points, name this Austrian symbolist.

This painter's drip technique was done by pouring paint onto canvases laid on the floor of a barn in Springs, New York. His works include Autumn Rhythm and Lavender Mist. A 1949 Life magazine article asked whether he was the greatest living painter in the United States. For 10 points, name this husband of Lee Krasner and leading Abstract Expressionist.

This artist's Seagram murals were painted for a restaurant but he withdrew from the commission. He is associated with Color Field painting, with rectangular blocks of luminous color in works like Orange and Yellow. A chapel in Houston houses fourteen of his dark canvases. For 10 points, name this Latvian-born American painter.

This French painter was criticized for his nude Olympia, which showed a prostitute staring directly at the viewer. His Luncheon on the Grass was shown at the 1863 Salon des Refuses. His last major work is A Bar at the Folies-Bergere. For 10 points, name this precursor of Impressionism.

A critic's review of this artist's Impression, Sunrise gave a movement its name. He painted series of haystacks and of Rouen Cathedral at different times of day. He painted giant water lilies in a garden at Giverny. For 10 points, name this French Impressionist.

This artist's pointillist masterpiece shows Parisians relaxing on an island in the Seine, with a monkey on a leash and a woman fishing. He worked on it for two years using tiny dots of complementary color. He also painted Bathers at Asnieres. For 10 points, name this French artist of A Sunday Afternoon on the Island of La Grande Jatte.

A critic named this movement after remarking that a Georges Braque painting looked like it was made of little cubes. It had Analytic and Synthetic phases, the latter incorporating collage. Les Demoiselles d'Avignon is its precursor. For 10 points, name this early twentieth-century movement of Braque and Picasso that fragmented objects into geometric planes.

This painter's Night Watch depicts a militia company led by Captain Frans Banninck Cocq. His Anatomy Lesson of Dr. Nicolaes Tulp shows a dissected arm. He painted dozens of self-portraits and went bankrupt in the 1650s. For 10 points, name this Dutch Golden Age artist.

This painter of The Milkmaid worked in Delft and used expensive ultramarine in works like Girl with a Pearl Earring. He painted a View of Delft showing clouds over the city. He left only about three dozen paintings. For 10 points, name this Dutch master of domestic light-filled interiors.

This sculptor created the Ecstasy of Saint Teresa for the Cornaro Chapel and the bronze baldacchino in Saint Peter's Basilica. His Apollo and Daphne shows a nymph turning into a laurel. He designed the colonnade of Saint Peter's Square. For 10 points, name this Italian Baroque sculptor.

This sculptor's The Burghers of Calais and The Gates of Hell were inspired by Dante. A figure from the latter was cast separately as The Thinker. His student and lover was Camille Claudel. For 10 points, name this French sculptor.

This Florentine sculptor's bronze David was commissioned by the Medici and shows the boy standing on Goliath's head, wearing a hat. His equestrian statue of the mercenary Gattamelata stands in Padua. He also made the relief Feast of Herod. For 10 points, name this early Renaissance sculptor.

This Mexican painter's The Two Fridas shows two versions of herself holding hands with exposed hearts. A bus accident left her in chronic pain. She lived in the Casa Azul in Coyoacan and was married twice to muralist Diego Rivera. For 10 points, name this painter of many self-portraits with a unibrow.

This artist painted melting clocks in The Persistence of Memory. He developed the "paranoiac-critical method" and collaborated with Luis Bunuel on Un chien andalou. He designed a theater-museum in Figueres. For 10 points, name this Spanish Surrealist known for a waxed, upturned mustache.

This Spanish court painter depicted a firing squad in The Third of May 1808. His print series Los Caprichos satirizes society, and his Black Paintings include Saturn Devouring His Son. He painted The Naked Maja. For 10 points, name this artist, Francisco de.

This Romantic painter's Liberty Leading the People shows a bare-breasted woman holding a tricolor flag over a barricade. His The Death of Sardanapalus and Massacre at Chios were also controversial. He rivaled Ingres, favoring color over line. For 10 points, name this Frenchman.

This neoclassical painter depicted a murdered revolutionary lying in his bathtub in The Death of Marat. His Oath of the Horatii used stern geometry to promote civic virtue. He later served as Napoleon's court painter for The Coronation of Napoleon. For 10 points, name this French artist, Jacques-Louis.

This Japanese ukiyo-e artist made Thirty-six Views of Mount Fuji. One print shows a huge wave about to engulf fishing boats off Kanagawa. He also produced fifteen volumes of sketches called manga. For 10 points, name this artist of The Great Wave.

This Russian painter co-founded the Blue Rider group with Franz Marc. His treatise Concerning the Spiritual in Art linked color to emotion and music. His Improvisations and Compositions are among the first purely abstract paintings. He taught at the Bauhaus. For 10 points, name this artist.

In his late years this artist, confined to a wheelchair, made the paper cutouts for Jazz and designed the Chapel of the Rosary in Vence. Earlier his Woman with a Hat shocked viewers at the 1905 Salon d'Automne, giving rise to a movement dubbed "wild beasts." His The Red Studio and The Dance use flat, saturated color. For 10 points, name this French leader of Fauvism.

This Pop artist's studio, the Factory, produced silkscreens of Marilyn Monroe and cans of Campbell's soup. His Brillo Box sculptures blurred the line between art and commerce. He managed the Velvet Underground. For 10 points, name this American artist.

This Norwegian painter's Frieze of Life includes Madonna and Vampire. His best-known painting shows a figure with hands on face on a bridge under a blood-red sky. Versions exist in painting and lithograph. For 10 points, name this painter of The Scream.

This Post-Impressionist from Aix-en-Provence painted Mont Sainte-Victoire repeatedly and The Card Players. He wanted to treat nature by the cylinder, the sphere, and the cone. His work influenced Picasso, who called him "the father of us all." For 10 points, name this French artist.

This American painter's enlarged flowers like Black Iris and bleached animal skulls such as Cow's Skull: Red, White and Blue made her famous. She moved to Ghost Ranch in New Mexico. Her husband, Alfred Stieglitz, photographed her extensively. For 10 points, name this modernist.

This Romanian-born sculptor's series Bird in Space reduces a bird to a gleaming upward curve. His Endless Column stands in Targu Jiu. He studied briefly under Rodin and then reduced forms to essentials, as in The Kiss. For 10 points, name this modernist who worked in Paris.

q: In this work's scherzo, timpani play a prominent role, and the finale begins with a recitative for cellos and basses that rejects earlier themes. The finale sets lines by Friedrich Schiller for four vocal soloists and chorus. It premiered in Vienna in 1824, with its deaf composer on stage. For 10 points, name this symphony in D minor whose "Ode to Joy" became the anthem of the European Union.

This composer wrote the Coffee Cantata and the Saint Matthew Passion. While serving the prince of Cothen he wrote his Brandenburg-era instrumental music, and later he improvised a three-part ricercar for Frederick the Great that grew into The Musical Offering. His B minor Mass was never performed complete in his lifetime. For 10 points, name this Lutheran composer from Eisenach, whose sons included Carl Philipp Emanuel.

This composer's final work was a Requiem left unfinished at his death in 1791 and completed by his pupil Franz Xaver Sussmayr. He wrote The Magic Flute, Don Giovanni, and The Marriage of Figaro. Ludwig von Kochel cataloged his output. For 10 points, name this child prodigy from Salzburg.

A riot allegedly broke out at the 1913 Paris premiere of this composer's The Rite of Spring, which had choreography by Nijinsky. He also wrote the ballets The Firebird and Petrushka for Diaghilev. Later he adopted a neoclassical style in works like The Rake's Progress. For 10 points, name this Russian-born composer.

This French composer wrote Prelude to the Afternoon of a Faun, inspired by a Mallarme poem. His opera Pelleas et Melisande and orchestral sketches La mer used whole-tone scales and blurred harmonies. His Suite bergamasque includes "Clair de lune." For 10 points, name this impressionist composer.

This composer wrote the operas Rigoletto, La traviata, and Il trovatore. His opera Aida was commissioned for a Cairo opera house. His chorus "Va, pensiero" from Nabucco became an Italian patriotic anthem. For 10 points, name this Italian composer of Otello and Falstaff.

This composer developed the leitmotif as a recurring theme linked to a character or idea. He built a festival theater at Bayreuth for his four-opera cycle about a cursed ring. His Tristan und Isolde uses a famous unresolved chord. For 10 points, name this German composer of The Ring of the Nibelung and "Ride of the Valkyries."

This Austrian composer died at age thirty-one but wrote over six hundred songs, including "Erlkonig," based on Goethe, and the cycle Winterreise. His Symphony No. 8 is called "Unfinished," and his Trout Quintet has a set of variations on his song. For 10 points, name this master of the Lied.

This composer's Piano Sonata No. 2 includes a funeral march as its third movement. He wrote a "Raindrop" prelude while staying on Majorca with George Sand. His heart was returned to Warsaw after his death in Paris in 1849. For 10 points, name this Polish piano composer of nocturnes and mazurkas.

This composer died in poverty in Vienna in 1741. His Gloria in D major and his collection L'estro armonico influenced Bach, who transcribed several of his concertos. Four violin concertos accompanied by sonnets depict the seasons. For 10 points, name this Italian Baroque composer.

This German-born composer moved to London and wrote the oratorio Messiah, whose "Hallelujah" chorus is traditionally heard standing. He also wrote Water Music for a royal barge party and Music for the Royal Fireworks. For 10 points, name this Baroque composer, George Frideric.

This composer wrote A German Requiem and the Academic Festival Overture. His four symphonies were slow in coming because he felt overshadowed by Beethoven. He championed his friend Robert Schumann's wife Clara. For 10 points, name this composer of Hungarian Dances and a famous lullaby.

This American composer wrote the ballets Rodeo, Billy the Kid, and Appalachian Spring, which quotes the Shaker tune "Simple Gifts." He wrote Fanfare for the Common Man. He studied with Nadia Boulanger in Paris. For 10 points, name this composer of the "Dean of American Music."

This work, premiered in 1924 by Paul Whiteman's band with its composer at the piano, opens with a clarinet glissando. It combined jazz idioms with classical forms. Its composer also wrote Porgy and Bess and An American in Paris. For 10 points, name this George Gershwin work whose title names a color.

This composer was denounced by Pravda in 1936 over his opera Lady Macbeth of the Mzensk District. His Symphony No. 5 was subtitled a "Soviet artist's response to just criticism." His Seventh Symphony, written during the siege of a city, is named for it. For 10 points, name this Soviet composer of the DSCH motif.

This composer's Piano Concerto No. 2 helped him recover after the failure of his first symphony. He wrote Rhapsody on a Theme of Paganini and the symphonic poem Isle of the Dead. He left Russia after the 1917 revolution and settled in the United States. For 10 points, name this pianist-composer with famously large hands.

This Austrian composer led the Vienna Court Opera and wrote Das Lied von der Erde and Kindertotenlieder. His Symphony No. 2 is nicknamed "Resurrection" and ends with a choral finale. His wife Alma was a composer and later married Gropius. For 10 points, name this Late Romantic.

This composer's best-known work is a one-movement orchestral piece built on a repeated snare-drum rhythm and a gradually growing crescendo. He also wrote Pavane for a Dead Princess and Mother Goose Suite. His left-hand piano concerto was written for Paul Wittgenstein. For 10 points, name this French composer of Bolero.

This composer spent most of his career working for the Esterhazy princes. His Symphony No. 94 includes a sudden loud chord after a quiet theme and is called "Surprise." He wrote The Creation and many string quartets, earning the title "Father of the Symphony." He taught Beethoven. For 10 points, name this Austrian composer.

This musical form has three main sections: an exposition presenting contrasting themes in different keys, a development that manipulates them, and a recapitulation returning to the home key. It is typical for the first movement of a symphony or sonata. For 10 points, name this structure, which shares its name with a multi-movement instrumental genre.

This contrapuntal composition begins with one voice stating a subject that is answered by other voices in imitation at a different pitch. Bach's The Art of this form remained unfinished. Its name comes from the Latin word for "flight." For 10 points, name this polyphonic form.

This New Orleans trumpeter led the Hot Five and Hot Seven bands and recorded "West End Blues." He popularized scat singing and was nicknamed "Satchmo." His late hits included "Hello, Dolly!" and "What a Wonderful World." For 10 points, name this jazz musician.

This bandleader played at Harlem's Cotton Club and composed "Mood Indigo" and "Sophisticated Lady." His longtime collaborator Billy Strayhorn wrote "Take the 'A' Train." He also wrote the extended work Black, Brown and Beige. For 10 points, name this jazz pianist and composer, Duke.

This trumpeter's 1959 album Kind of Blue is based on modal improvisation and features John Coltrane and Bill Evans. He also recorded Birth of the Cool and electric albums such as Bitches Brew. For 10 points, name this jazz innovator.

This saxophonist recorded the harmonically dense Giant Steps and a suite in four parts that begins with "Acknowledgement." His playing in the 1950s was described as "sheets of sound." He also recorded "My Favorite Things" on soprano saxophone. For 10 points, name this jazz musician who made A Love Supreme.

This group from Liverpool made Sergeant Pepper's Lonely Hearts Club Band and Abbey Road. They appeared on The Ed Sullivan Show in 1964. Producer George Martin worked with them, and members included John Lennon, Paul McCartney, George Harrison, and Ringo Starr. For 10 points, name this British band.

This composer wrote Eugene Onegin and the ballet Swan Lake. His 1812 Overture calls for cannon fire. His Symphony No. 6, subtitled "Pathetique," ends with a slow movement and premiered nine days before his death in 1893. His patron was Nadezhda von Meck. For 10 points, name this Russian composer.

This Russian composer was a member of The Five, the "Mighty Handful." His opera Boris Godunov deals with the tsar's guilt. A piano suite of his depicts walking through a gallery of Viktor Hartmann's paintings, with the "Promenade" theme linking movements. For 10 points, name this composer of Pictures at an Exhibition and Night on Bald Mountain.

This Hungarian composer collected folk songs with Zoltan Kodaly and used them in his work. He wrote Mikrokosmos, a set of 153 piano pieces, and the opera Duke Bluebeard's Castle. He fled to the United States before World War II and wrote a Concerto for Orchestra. For 10 points, name this composer.

This Austrian composer developed a method of composing using all twelve chromatic pitches in a fixed row. He used Sprechstimme in Pierrot lunaire and wrote Verklarte Nacht. With Berg and Webern, he formed the Second Viennese School. He fled the Nazis and settled in Los Angeles. For 10 points, name this composer.

q: This Swedish director's The Seventh Seal depicts a knight, Antonius Block, playing chess with Death. His Persona stars Liv Ullmann and Bibi Andersson, and Wild Strawberries follows an aged professor on a road trip. He often worked with cinematographer Sven Nykvist and shot on Faro Island. For 10 points, name this director.

This Italian director's 8 1/2 follows a filmmaker named Guido, played by Marcello Mastroianni, who struggles with creative block. La Dolce Vita includes a scene in the Trevi Fountain. His composer was Nino Rota. For 10 points, name this director of La Strada and Amarcord.

This director's 1960 debut feature has Jean-Paul Belmondo as a petty criminal who imitates Humphrey Bogart and Jean Seberg as an American student in Paris. He wrote criticism for Cahiers du cinema before directing Contempt and Weekend. His editing used jump cuts. For 10 points, name this French New Wave filmmaker of Breathless.

This director's first feature follows the delinquent Antoine Doinel, played by Jean-Pierre Leaud, and ends with a freeze frame on a beach. He also directed Jules and Jim and Day for Night. He wrote an essay attacking the "tradition of quality" in French cinema. For 10 points, name this director of The 400 Blows.

Associated with critics at Cahiers du cinema such as Eric Rohmer, Jacques Rivette, and Claude Chabrol, this film movement emerged in the late 1950s. It favored location shooting, handheld cameras, and a personal style influenced by the "auteur theory." It broke with the studio-bound tradition of French cinema. For 10 points, name this movement whose name translates as "Nouvelle Vague."

Directors such as Roberto Rossellini and Vittorio De Sica led this postwar movement in Italy. Rome, Open City and Bicycle Thieves used location shooting, natural light, and many nonprofessional actors. Its films depicted the poverty and hardship of ordinary people after World War II. For 10 points, name this Italian film movement.

This film movement of the 1920s Weimar Republic used distorted sets, harsh shadows, and painted-on lighting. Examples include The Cabinet of Dr. Caligari by Robert Wiene and Murnau's Nosferatu. It influenced later film noir and horror films. For 10 points, name this German style.

In this 1958 film, a detective with acrophobia is hired to follow a woman who seems possessed by a dead ancestor. James Stewart plays Scottie Ferguson, and Kim Novak plays both Madeleine and Judy. The film is famous for a camera effect that simultaneously tracks backward and zooms forward. For 10 points, name this Alfred Hitchcock film set in San Francisco.

This effect named for a Soviet filmmaker shows how viewers derive meaning from editing. A neutral close-up of an actor's face was cut together with a bowl of soup, a coffin, and a woman, and audiences read different emotions into the same face. It is a cornerstone of montage theory. For 10 points, name this film editing effect named for Lev.

This French term, meaning "placing on stage," names everything visible in the frame: sets, costumes, lighting, actor positions, and props. Critics at Cahiers du cinema analyzed it in the work of auteurs. It is often contrasted with montage. For 10 points, name this term for visual composition within a shot.

This director pioneered cross-cutting for last-minute rescues in his Biograph shorts. His epic Intolerance interweaves four stories across different eras, and his earlier 1915 film is both a landmark in technique and notorious for racism. He co-founded United Artists. For 10 points, name this American silent film director, D. W.

This Bengali director's debut Pather Panchali began a trilogy about a boy named Apu, followed by Aparajito and The World of Apu. He also made Charulata. He won an honorary Oscar shortly before he died in 1992. For 10 points, name this Indian director from Calcutta.

This Japanese director's Tokyo Story follows an elderly couple visiting their children. He often placed the camera at a low height, as if viewing from a tatami mat, and used "pillow shots" of still objects between scenes. He often cast Setsuko Hara. For 10 points, name this director of Late Spring.

This Soviet director made Solaris, Stalker, and Mirror. His book Sculpting in Time outlines his view of the long take as shaping time. His first feature, Ivan's Childhood, won the Golden Lion in Venice in 1962, and his Andrei Rublev depicts a medieval icon painter. For 10 points, name this director.

This German director's Aguirre, the Wrath of God and Fitzcarraldo both starred the volatile Klaus Kinski. During the making of the latter, a steamship was hauled up a hill in the Peruvian jungle. His documentaries include Grizzly Man and Cave of Forgotten Dreams. For 10 points, name this director.

This Soviet filmmaker's 1929 work Man with a Movie Camera uses double exposures, split screens, and freeze frames to portray a day in the life of a city. He developed the "Kino-Eye" theory and led the Kinoks group. For 10 points, name this documentary pioneer, born David Kaufman.

This American filmmaker's 1922 documentary follows an Inuk hunter and his family in northern Quebec. Parts were staged, which sparked debate over documentary ethics. He later made Man of Aran and Louisiana Story. For 10 points, name this man who made Nanook of the North.

This term names the live recording of everyday sounds such as footsteps and door slams that are added to film in post-production. A studio stage may feature surfaces such as gravel and wood. Coconut shells are classically used to simulate horse hooves. It is named for a Universal Studios sound pioneer, Jack. For 10 points, give this term for sound-effects artistry.

This Italian composer scored Sergio Leone's Dollars trilogy, including The Good, the Bad and the Ugly, with coyote-like howls and whistling. He also wrote the music for Once Upon a Time in the West and The Mission. He won a competitive Oscar for The Hateful Eight. For 10 points, name this composer.

This composer scored Alfred Hitchcock's Psycho using only string instruments, with shrieking violins in the shower scene. He also scored Citizen Kane, North by Northwest, and Taxi Driver. A theremin features in his score for The Day the Earth Stood Still. For 10 points, name this American film composer.

This photographer ran the gallery 291 and edited the journal Camera Work, promoting the Photo-Secession. His 1907 picture The Steerage shows passengers on an ocean liner. His series Equivalents consists of photographs of clouds. For 10 points, name this photographer who was married to Georgia O'Keeffe.

This French photographer co-founded the Magnum agency in 1947 and coined the idea of the "decisive moment." His image Behind the Gare Saint-Lazare shows a man leaping over a puddle. He used a small Leica rangefinder. For 10 points, name this photojournalist, Henri.

This photographer's square-format images include Identical Twins, Roselle, New Jersey. She photographed giants, nudists, and people on society's margins, often at close range. She died by suicide in 1971, a year before a posthumous Venice Biennale showing. For 10 points, name this American photographer.

This artist's Untitled Film Stills, made from 1977 to 1980, show her posing as various female stereotypes from imaginary movies. She often acts as her own model, costumed and made up. She is associated with the Pictures Generation. For 10 points, name this American photographer.

This American artist in Paris made rayographs by placing objects directly on photographic paper. His Le Violon d'Ingres adds f-holes to a woman's back. He associated with Dada and Surrealism and collaborated with Marcel Duchamp. For 10 points, name this American Dada and Surrealist photographer.

This Hungarian-born photographer's blurred images of troops landing at Omaha Beach on D-Day survive only in a few frames. He photographed The Falling Soldier during the Spanish Civil War and co-founded Magnum. He was killed by a landmine in Indochina in 1954. For 10 points, name this war photographer.

This New York photographer with a studio on Broadway photographed Lincoln before a Cooper Union speech. During the Civil War, his teams captured battlefield scenes, including Antietam and Gettysburg. His staff included Alexander Gardner. For 10 points, name this documenter of the Civil War, Mathew.

This American cartoonist created the comic strip Little Nemo in Slumberland. His 1914 animated film features a dinosaur that interacts with him on stage in vaudeville. He also made The Sinking of the Lusitania. For 10 points, name this animator of Gertie the Dinosaur.

This Japanese artist founded Mushi Production and created Astro Boy, the first popular anime TV series. His Kimba the White Lion is a precursor of Disney's later hit with a lion. He is called the "God of Manga." For 10 points, name this creator.

This German animator made The Adventures of Prince Achmed in 1926, one of the earliest surviving feature-length animated films. She cut out figures from black paper and filmed their silhouettes on glass lit from below. Her husband Carl Koch collaborated. For 10 points, name this pioneer of silhouette animation, Lotte.
Answer these questions about film editing.
parts: What term names a rapid sequence of short shots that condenses time or conveys an idea?

q: This architect designed the Queen's House at Greenwich and the Banqueting House in Whitehall. He laid out the Covent Garden piazza and designed masque sets for Ben Jonson. After visiting Italy, he introduced the Palladian style to England. For 10 points, name this seventeenth-century English architect.

After a fire in 1194, this Gothic cathedral southwest of Paris was rebuilt with flying buttresses and tall stained-glass windows. A labyrinth is inlaid in the floor of its nave. Its two unmatched spires differ in style. For 10 points, name this French cathedral whose blue glass is much admired.

This architect designed the Salk Institute in La Jolla, with its central courtyard opening toward the Pacific. His Kimbell Art Museum in Fort Worth uses cycloid vaults to diffuse light. He designed the National Assembly in Dhaka and spoke of "silence and light." For 10 points, name this American architect of the Indian Institute of Management Ahmedabad.

This German architect and his partner Adolf Meyer designed the glass-walled Fagus Factory. He founded the Bauhaus and designed its Dessau building. After emigrating to America he taught at Harvard and designed his own house in Lincoln, Massachusetts. For 10 points, name this modernist.

This Finnish-born American designed the Gateway Arch in Saint Louis and the TWA Flight Center at Kennedy Airport. His Tulip chair is a classic of mid-century furniture. He designed the main terminal at Dulles Airport and was the son of another architect. For 10 points, name this architect, Eero.

This architect designed the Glass House in New Canaan, Connecticut, and was the first winner of the Pritzker Prize. He collaborated with Mies on the Seagram Building and designed the AT&T Building with its Chippendale-style top. He curated MoMA's 1932 International Style exhibition. For 10 points, name this American architect.

This Italian architect and his British partner Richard Rogers designed the Pompidou Centre, with color-coded pipes on the exterior. He also designed the Shard in London and the Kansai International Airport terminal. For 10 points, name this architect, Renzo.

This British architect designed the glass dome of the Reichstag in Berlin and the HSBC building in Hong Kong. His 30 Saint Mary Axe in London is nicknamed the Gherkin. He also designed the Millau Viaduct and Apple Park. For 10 points, name this architect, Norman.

Le Corbusier's Unite d'Habitation and Boston City Hall exemplify this style. Its name comes from the French for "raw concrete." It features exposed concrete, massive forms, and repeating modular elements. Alison and Peter Smithson helped name it. For 10 points, name this style of postwar architecture.

This style flourished from about 1890 to 1910 and used sinuous plant-like lines. Victor Horta's Hotel Tassel in Brussels is an early example. Hector Guimard designed its cast-iron entrances to the Paris Metro. Mackintosh designed the Glasgow School of Art in this style. For 10 points, name this decorative style, "the new art."

Borromini's San Carlo alle Quattro Fontane is an example of this style, with undulating walls and oval plans. It flourished after the Council of Trent, emphasizing drama, movement, and light. Versailles and Bernini's work belong to this style. For 10 points, name this style that followed the Renaissance and preceded the Rococo.

This Loire Valley palace was begun under Francis I as a hunting lodge. It has a double-helix staircase often attributed to Leonardo da Vinci's ideas. Its roofline bristles with chimneys and turrets. For 10 points, name this large French chateau, whose name begins with C.

This building has a forest of columns supporting double-tiered red-and-white striped horseshoe arches. Begun by Abd al-Rahman I, it was converted into a cathedral after the Reconquista, with a Renaissance nave inserted into the center. For 10 points, name this former mosque in an Andalusian city.

This temple complex was built by the Khmer king Suryavarman II and dedicated to Vishnu. Its five towers rise in a quincunx and reliefs show the churning of the ocean of milk. It was later used by Buddhists. For 10 points, name this Cambodian temple.

This Buddhist monument in Java was built under the Sailendra dynasty. Nine stacked platforms are topped with a central stupa surrounded by seventy-two smaller bell-shaped stupas. Its galleries show relief carvings of the life of the Buddha. For 10 points, name this Indonesian monument.

On the spring and autumn equinoxes, the shadow of this pyramid's balustrade forms a serpent that appears to slither down its staircase. It stands at a Maya city in the Yucatan Peninsula near a large ball court. It has 91 steps on each of four sides plus a top platform. For 10 points, name this pyramid dedicated to Kukulcan.

This Nabataean capital in Jordan is entered by walking through a narrow canyon called the Siq. Its most famous facade, Al-Khazneh, or "the Treasury," is carved out of rose-colored sandstone. It appears in Indiana Jones and the Last Crusade. For 10 points, name this "rose-red city."

Ivan the Terrible commissioned this church in Moscow to commemorate the capture of Kazan. It has nine chapels grouped around a central tower, and its onion domes are brightly colored. It stands at the edge of Red Square. For 10 points, name this Russian Orthodox cathedral.

Construction of this bell tower in the Piazza dei Miracoli began in 1173, and it began leaning because of soft ground. It was stabilized in a project completed in 2001. Legend says Galileo dropped weights from it. For 10 points, name this tower in an Italian city.

After a fire in 1834 destroyed the old building, this architect rebuilt the Palace of Westminster in Gothic Revival style. Augustus Pugin designed the interiors and the clock tower, which houses Big Ben. He also designed the Reform Club in the style of an Italian palazzo. For 10 points, name this British architect, Charles.

This architect directed the construction of the "White City" at the 1893 World's Columbian Exposition. He designed the Flatiron Building in New York and Union Station in Washington. He is associated with the Plan of Chicago and the line "Make no little plans." For 10 points, name this American architect, Daniel.

This New York park was laid out by Frederick Law Olmsted and Calvert Vaux in the 1850s under the Greensward Plan. It has sunken transverse roads that carry cross-town traffic out of sight. Bethesda Terrace and Sheep Meadow are features. For 10 points, name this park in Manhattan.

This president designed his home at Monticello and the Rotunda of the University of Virginia, based on the Pantheon. He modeled the Virginia State Capitol on the Maison Carree in Nimes. He also wrote the Declaration of Independence. For 10 points, name this third president and amateur architect.

This architect's book Complexity and Contradiction in Architecture answered Mies's maxim by saying "less is a bore." He co-wrote Learning from Las Vegas with Denise Scott Brown and Steven Izenour. He designed a house for his mother and the Sainsbury Wing of the National Gallery. For 10 points, name this postmodern architect.

This Finnish architect designed the Paimio Sanatorium and Villa Mairea, and Finlandia Hall in Helsinki. His bentwood furniture was produced by Artek, a company he co-founded. His wavy glass Savoy vase is a design icon. For 10 points, name this Scandinavian modernist, Alvar.

This self-taught Japanese architect, a former boxer, designed the Church of the Light with a cross-shaped slit in a concrete wall. He won the Pritzker Prize in 1995. His work uses exposed concrete and natural light. For 10 points, name this architect of the Church on the Water.

This Spanish architect and engineer designed the Turning Torso in Malmo and the Quadracci Pavilion at the Milwaukee Art Museum, whose wings open and close. His Oculus transit hub in New York has a winged form. He built the Alamillo Bridge in Seville. For 10 points, name this architect.

This Dutch architect's firm OMA designed the Seattle Central Library and the CCTV Headquarters in Beijing. He wrote Delirious New York. He won the Pritzker Prize in 2000. For 10 points, name this architect, Rem.

This Paris building by Charles Garnier was designed in the Beaux-Arts style after a competition won by its unknown young architect in 1861. Its Grand Staircase is lined with marble, and the auditorium ceiling was painted by Chagall. It is the setting of Gaston Leroux's The Phantom of the Opera. For 10 points, name this Paris opera house.

This palace complex in Beijing was built under the Yongle Emperor in the early fifteenth century and housed Ming and Qing emperors. Its central axis runs through the Meridian Gate to the Hall of Supreme Harmony. Its buildings have yellow glazed tile roofs. For 10 points, name this imperial palace.

q: In this play, Pozzo arrives leading Lucky on a rope, and a boy brings word that the one being awaited will not come today. Two tramps named Vladimir and Estragon wait by a barren tree, frequently saying "Nothing to be done." It was first written in French by Samuel Beckett and premiered in Paris in 1953. For 10 points, name this play about waiting for a man named Godot.

At the end of this 1879 play, the heroine slams the door on her husband Torvald Helmer after he reacts badly to her having forged a signature. Nora Helmer dances a tarantella at a Christmas party, and Krogstad blackmails her. For 10 points, name this play by Henrik Ibsen whose title names a dwelling and a toy.

The Moscow Art Theatre staged the first successful production of this dramatist's The Seagull, directed by Stanislavski. He also wrote Uncle Vanya, Three Sisters, and The Cherry Orchard. He trained as a physician and wrote many short stories. For 10 points, name this Russian author.

Willy Loman is a traveling salesman who has hallucinations of his brother Ben, and his sons are Biff and Happy. His wife Linda says "attention must be paid" to him. The play ends with his funeral after a car crash suicide. For 10 points, name this 1949 Arthur Miller play.

Marlon Brando played Stanley Kowalski in the 1951 film of this play, set in New Orleans on Elysian Fields Street. Stella's sister Blanche DuBois ends by saying that she has "always depended on the kindness of strangers." It premiered on Broadway in 1947. For 10 points, name this Tennessee Williams play named for a form of transportation.

This Polish director founded the Laboratory Theatre in Wroclaw and wrote Towards a Poor Theatre. He stripped away costumes, sets, and lighting to focus on the actor's physical and spiritual work. His actor Ryszard Cieslak starred in The Constant Prince. For 10 points, name this theater practitioner.

This French writer called for a "Theatre of Cruelty" that would assault the audience's senses, as set out in his book The Theatre and Its Double. He broke with the Surrealists and spent years in asylums such as Rodez. He was inspired by Balinese theater. For 10 points, name this French theorist.

Martin Esslin coined this label in 1961 for a group of dramatists including Ionesco, Genet, and Pinter. Its plays often feature illogical dialogue, circular plots, and characters in meaningless situations. Camus's essay on Sisyphus supplied its philosophical background. For 10 points, name this movement in postwar theater.

This Athenian tragedian wrote Medea, The Trojan Women, and The Bacchae. He was often accused of making his gods into dei ex machina to resolve plots. He wrote about women's psychology in plays such as Hippolytus. For 10 points, name this contemporary of Sophocles.

This Elizabethan playwright wrote Tamburlaine the Great and The Jew of Malta. His Doctor Faustus has the line "Was this the face that launched a thousand ships?" He was stabbed in a tavern in Deptford in 1593. For 10 points, name this playwright who developed blank verse before Shakespeare.

This French playwright, born Jean-Baptiste Poquelin, wrote Tartuffe and The Misanthrope. He died in 1673 after collapsing during a performance of his play The Imaginary Invalid. His company performed at the Palais-Royal under Louis XIV's patronage. For 10 points, name this comic dramatist.

Nicknamed "the Divine," this French actress starred in Phedre and Victorien Sardou's La Tosca and played the male roles of Hamlet and L'Aiglon. She had her leg amputated in 1915 but kept performing. She appeared with the Comedie-Francaise. For 10 points, name this actress, Sarah.

This American actor played Hamlet for one hundred consecutive nights in 1864 and 1865 in New York. He founded The Players club in Gramercy Park. His brother assassinated Abraham Lincoln. For 10 points, name this nineteenth-century Shakespearean actor, Edwin.

This French-born choreographer worked for decades in Saint Petersburg and led the Imperial Ballet. He choreographed The Sleeping Beauty, La Bayadere, and Raymonda. He collaborated with Lev Ivanov on Swan Lake and The Nutcracker. For 10 points, name this "father of classical ballet."

This dancer was famous for his enormous leaps and for the role of the Golden Slave and for Le Spectre de la rose. He choreographed Afternoon of a Faun, which shocked Paris with an erotic gesture in 1912. He later suffered a mental breakdown and was institutionalized. For 10 points, name this Ballets Russes star, Vaslav.

This American dancer rejected the formal ballet technique, dancing barefoot in loose Greek-style tunics. She founded schools in Germany and Russia and died in 1927 when her long scarf caught in a car's wheel. She was a pioneer of modern dance. For 10 points, name this dancer, Isadora.

This choreographer founded his own company in 1953 and used chance procedures influenced by I Ching to decide the order of movements. He collaborated with composer John Cage and artist Robert Rauschenberg. He first danced with Martha Graham. For 10 points, name this American choreographer, Merce.

This choreographer's style includes bowler hats, white gloves, turned-in knees, and isolated hip movements. He directed the film version of Cabaret and choreographed Chicago and Pippin on Broadway. His semi-autobiographical film All That Jazz won awards. For 10 points, name this man who created "Steam Heat" in The Pajama Game.

This choreographer's Fancy Free, about three sailors on leave, was expanded into the musical On the Town. He staged the dances of West Side Story and was ballet master of the New York City Ballet. He later testified before the House Un-American Activities Committee. For 10 points, name this American choreographer, Jerome.

This dancer defected from the Soviet Union in 1961 at Le Bourget airport in Paris. A famous partnership with Margot Fonteyn at the Royal Ballet began soon afterward. He later directed the Paris Opera Ballet. For 10 points, name this Kirov dancer, Rudolf.

This Latvian-born dancer defected in 1974 while on tour in Toronto. He became a principal at American Ballet Theatre and later directed it. He also appeared in the film The Turning Point and in television's Sex and the City. For 10 points, name this dancer, Mikhail.

This German choreographer led the Tanztheater Wuppertal, merging dance and theater. Her works include Cafe Muller and a 1975 version of The Rite of Spring on a stage covered with peat. Wim Wenders made a 3-D documentary film about her in 2011. For 10 points, name this choreographer, Pina.

This classical Indian dance from Tamil Nadu uses elaborate hand gestures called mudras and the half-sitting position araimandi. It grew out of temple dance performed by devadasis and was revived in the twentieth century by Rukmini Devi Arundale. For 10 points, name this dance form whose name is traditionally broken into bhava, raga, tala, and natya.

This Chinese theater form combines singing, mime, acrobatics, and martial arts. Performers wear colored face paint, and roles are divided into sheng, dan, jing, and chou. Mei Lanfang was a famed male performer of female roles. For 10 points, name this theater form associated with the capital.

In this Indonesian art, a dalang manipulates flat leather puppets behind a lit white screen, accompanied by a gamelan orchestra. Stories are often drawn from the Ramayana and Mahabharata. It is especially associated with Java and Bali. For 10 points, name this shadow puppet theater whose name means "shadow" in Javanese.

This Saint Petersburg jeweler made a series of jeweled eggs for the Russian imperial family as Easter gifts, beginning with the Hen Egg. Each held a "surprise." Carl Peter made the series for Alexander III and Nicholas II. For 10 points, name this house of jewelers.

This American designer developed Favrile glass, an iridescent glass used in vases and lamps. His leaded-glass lamps, such as the Wisteria lamp, are collector's items. He decorated the Seventh Regiment Armory and created Laurelton Hall. He was the son of a famous New York jeweler. For 10 points, name this Art Nouveau artist, Louis Comfort.

This English potter developed Jasperware, with white classical reliefs on a blue background. He produced Queen's Ware and made copies of the Portland Vase. He was an abolitionist who made an anti-slavery medallion. His grandson was Charles Darwin. For 10 points, name this founder of a Staffordshire pottery company.

A 2002 exhibition at the Museum of Fine Arts, Houston, brought national attention to the quilts of this small Alabama community along a river. Quilters such as Annie Mae Young and members of the Pettway family made improvisational geometric designs. The community was formerly a cotton plantation. For 10 points, name this community whose quilts are held in museums.

This work of embroidered wool on linen is about seventy meters long. It depicts the lead-up to the Norman Conquest and includes a scene of Halley's Comet, a Latin text, and a border with animals. Its main scenes show the Battle of Hastings. For 10 points, name this medieval work, named for a Norman town.

q: Cairo, Illinois, sits at the confluence where the Ohio River joins this river. Its headwaters are at Lake Itasca in Minnesota, and it passes Saint Paul, Saint Louis, and Memphis. Its delta lies south of New Orleans. For 10 points, name this river that empties into the Gulf of Mexico.

This river is formed by the confluence of the Allegheny and Monongahela Rivers at Pittsburgh. It forms the southern border of Ohio, Indiana, and Illinois. Cincinnati and Louisville lie on its banks. For 10 points, name this river that meets the Mississippi at Cairo, Illinois.

Its headwaters lie at Three Forks, Montana, where the Jefferson, Madison, and Gallatin Rivers meet. Lewis and Clark followed it upstream, passing the site of Great Falls. It flows past Omaha and Kansas City before joining the Mississippi north of Saint Louis. For 10 points, name this river nicknamed the "Big Muddy."

Elephant Butte Reservoir in New Mexico is on this river, which also flows through Albuquerque. Big Bend National Park is carved by a great loop of it. Ciudad Juarez lies across it from El Paso. For 10 points, name this river that forms much of the Texas-Mexico border.

The Glen Canyon Dam impounds Lake Powell on this river, and the Hoover Dam impounds Lake Mead. It begins in the Rocky Mountains of Colorado and carves the Grand Canyon. Its modern delta is in Mexico near the Gulf of California. For 10 points, name this river of the American Southwest.

The Grand Coulee Dam and Bonneville Dam are on this river, which is joined by the Snake River. It forms much of the border between Washington and Oregon. It enters the Pacific Ocean near Astoria. For 10 points, name this river of the Pacific Northwest.
